briefing.title: The Roman Empire, AD 284
paragraphs: In AD 284 the Roman Empire stretches from Britain to Syria, but it is falling apart. For half a century invasions, revolts and short-lived emperors have battered it. On a hill near Nicomedia, in north-western Turkey, the army hails a new emperor: Diocletian, a soldier of humble birth from Dalmatia on the Adriatic coast.

Can one man hold it all together? Diocletian will try sharing power among four rulers, heavy new taxes and a war on Christians. Then a young officer, Constantine, will fight his way to sole rule and make Rome Christian.

timelines.name: Level 1: The Big Turning Points
timelines.blurb: Four key moments from Diocletian's rise to Constantine's new capital.

events.label: Army hails Diocles as emperor
events.fact: On a hill about 5 km (three miles) outside Nicomedia the troops proclaimed him, and he took the name Diocletian.

events.label: Two Caesars join the two Augusti
events.fact: Galerius took the East and Constantine's father took Gaul and Britain, creating the Tetrarchy, or 'rule by four'.

events.label: Maxentius drowns at the Milvian Bridge
events.fact: His temporary bridge of boats collapsed as Constantine's troops drove his army into the Tiber.

events.label: Constantinople is dedicated
events.fact: Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantium as 'Constantine's City', a capital for more than a thousand years.

timelines.name: Level 2: Building and Breaking a System
timelines.blurb: Six events from the crisis to the Edict of Milan.

events.label: Crisis of the Third Century begins
events.fact: An age of invasions, revolts and short-lived emperors began long before Diocletian took power.

events.label: Maximian becomes Augustus of the West
events.fact: Diocletian's fellow officer became a full co-emperor, while Diocletian stayed senior partner in the East.

events.label: Peace of Nisibis with Persia
events.fact: After Galerius's victories, this lasting peace brought Armenia back under Roman influence.

events.label: Edict on Maximum Prices issued
events.fact: It set top prices for more than a thousand goods but drove trade into a black market.

events.label: Diocletian steps down
events.fact: He became the first Roman emperor to retire voluntarily, and Maximian resigned the same day in Milan.

events.label: Edict of Milan agreed
events.fact: Constantine and his eastern co-emperor granted freedom of worship to all religions.

timelines.name: Level 3: Fifty Years of Upheaval
timelines.blurb: Eight events from Diocletian's first victory to Constantine's death.

events.label: Diocletian wins near the river Margus
events.fact: He defeated the western emperor near the Margus, in modern Serbia.

events.label: Galerius takes Ctesiphon
events.fact: Striking through Armenia, Galerius seized the Persian capital on the Tigris along with the king's treasury and wife.

events.label: Soldiers tear down Nicomedia's church
events.fact: This opened the Great Persecution; the next day an edict ordered churches and holy books destroyed empire-wide.

events.label: Troops at York proclaim Constantine
events.fact: When his father died at York, the soldiers hailed Constantine Augustus, though Galerius recognised him only as Caesar.

events.label: Diocletian refuses a comeback
events.fact: Begged to return at Carnuntum, an army town on the Danube, he said they would never ask if they saw his cabbages.

events.label: Maximian dies at Marseille
events.fact: After rebelling against his son-in-law Constantine, he was cornered at Marseille and hanged himself.

events.label: Bishops meet at Nicaea
events.fact: Summoned by Constantine, the bishops produced the Nicene Creed, a statement of Christian belief.

events.label: Constantine dies near Nicomedia
events.fact: Baptised only on his deathbed, he left the empire to his sons, replacing rule by four with rule by family.

matchSets.name: Titles of the Tetrarchy
matchSets.blurb: Match each term to its meaning in Diocletian's new style of rule.

pairs.name: Tetrarchy
pairs.match: From a Greek word meaning 'rule by four'

pairs.name: Caesar
pairs.match: Junior emperor, meant to step up when the senior pair retired

pairs.name: adoratio
pairs.match: Lying face down before the emperor

pairs.name: Iovius
pairs.match: Diocletian's title, after Jupiter, king of the gods

pairs.name: Herculius
pairs.match: Maximian's title, after Jupiter's heroic helper

matchSets.name: Edicts, Treaties and Symbols
matchSets.blurb: Match each name to what it did or meant.

pairs.name: Edict on Maximum Prices
pairs.match: Set top prices for more than a thousand goods in 301

pairs.name: Edict of Milan
pairs.match: Granted freedom of worship to all religions in 313

pairs.name: Peace of Nisibis
pairs.match: Lasting peace with Persia that returned Armenia to Roman influence

pairs.name: solidus
pairs.match: Gold coin that kept its weight and purity for seven centuries

trueFalseDecks.name: Diocletian's Empire
trueFalseDecks.blurb: True or false: the soldier-emperor and his rule by four.

cards.claim: Diocletian was born in Dalmatia with the name Diocles.
cards.why: He was born around AD 243 in Dalmatia, on the Adriatic coast, and was plain Diocles until he became emperor.

cards.claim: In 285 Diocletian defeated the western emperor near the river Rhine.
cards.why: The battle was near the river Margus in modern Serbia.

cards.claim: The word Tetrarchy comes from a Greek word meaning 'rule by four'.
cards.why: From 293 two senior emperors (Augusti) and two junior emperors (Caesars) shared power.

cards.claim: In 297 Galerius won a crushing victory over the Persians in northern Mesopotamia.
cards.why: In 297 the Persians crushed Galerius; he only struck back successfully in 298 through Armenia.

cards.claim: Diocletian cut the number of provinces to about fifty.
cards.why: He doubled them, from about fifty to almost a hundred, so no governor could easily rebel.

cards.claim: The Edict on Maximum Prices stayed in force for decades.
cards.why: Goods slipped into a black market and the edict was dropped, perhaps within a year.

cards.claim: In 303 soldiers tore down the new church at Nicomedia and burned its scriptures.
cards.why: On 23 February 303 they destroyed the new church and burned its scriptures; an empire-wide edict followed the next day.

cards.claim: Diocletian retired to a fortified palace that is now the old heart of Split.
cards.why: His palace on the Dalmatian coast forms the old centre of Split in Croatia.

trueFalseDecks.name: Constantine's Road to Power
trueFalseDecks.blurb: True or false: from Naissus to Constantinople.

cards.claim: Constantine was born at Naissus, now Niš in Serbia.
cards.why: He was born there around AD 272; his mother was a woman of humble birth.

cards.claim: Constantine's father died at Milan, where the troops proclaimed Constantine Augustus.
cards.why: His father died at York on 25 July 306, and the troops there proclaimed him.

cards.claim: Constantine crossed the Alps with about 40,000 men in 312.
cards.why: Against his advisers' warnings he invaded Italy and won battles near Turin and at Verona.

cards.claim: Maxentius drowned when a temporary bridge of boats collapsed.
cards.why: His army was driven toward the Tiber by the Milvian Bridge, and the bridge of boats gave way.

cards.claim: The two Christian writers who knew Constantine told the same story of his vision.
cards.why: They told different stories: a dream about shields, or a cross of light above the sun followed by a dream.

cards.claim: The Senate's arch to Constantine's victory is covered in Christian symbols.
cards.why: The arch shows no Christian symbols at all.

cards.claim: Constantine dedicated Constantinople in 330 on the site of Byzantium.
cards.why: He refounded the Greek city on the strait between Europe and Asia as 'Constantine's City'.

cards.claim: Constantine was baptised as a young man at Diocletian's court.
cards.why: He was baptised only on his deathbed, in 337.

oddOneOut.why: Diocletian, Maximian and Galerius were among the four tetrarchs of 293. Maxentius, Maximian's son, was passed over and later seized Rome.
Galerius seized the treasury, the king's wife and the capital Ctesiphon in 298. Alexandria in Egypt was besieged and taken by Diocletian.
Doubling the provinces, the five-yearly census and taxing Italy were Diocletian's reforms. The Edict of Milan was agreed by Constantine in 313.
Destroying churches, burning scriptures and banning worship were measures of the Great Persecution. Returning property came with the Edict of Milan.
Constantine fought near Turin, at Verona and at the Milvian Bridge in 312. The Margus was where Diocletian won in 285.

items: Dream before battle to paint shields
Cross of light above the sun
oddOneOut.why: The cross of light, the words and the labarum come from the bishop's grander tale. The dream about painting shields is the Christian teacher's version.
Refounding Byzantium, calling the bishops to Nicaea and creating the solidus were Constantine's acts. Diocletian besieged Alexandria in 297-298.

whoAmI.name: Rulers of the Tetrarchy
whoAmI.blurb: Which emperor of the rule by four am I?

people.name: Diocletian
clues: Ancient writers called my father either a scribe or a freed slave.
I besieged Alexandria until it fell in 298.
I styled myself Iovius, after Jupiter, king of the gods.
Begged to return to power in 308, I pointed to the cabbages I had planted.

people.name: Maximian
clues: I resigned in Milan on the same day my senior partner stepped down.
In the West I ignored the later edicts against Christians.
On 1 April 286 I became Augustus, ruling the West.
I took the name Herculius, after Jupiter's heroic helper.

people.name: Galerius
clues: Near death in 311, I called off the persecution of Christians, admitting it had failed.
In 298 I struck through Armenia and took Ctesiphon, the Persian capital.
After the Persians crushed me in 297, I had to walk ahead of the imperial procession in purple.
I became Caesar of the East in 293 as Diocletian's son-in-law.

people.name: Constantine
clues: I was born around AD 272 at Naissus, now Niš in Serbia.
My troops proclaimed me Augustus at York after my father died.
In 330 I dedicated a refounded Byzantium as my own city.
I won at the Milvian Bridge, where my rival drowned in the Tiber.

people.name: Maxentius
clues: Twice I beat invaders by holding out behind Rome's walls.
I took the Sibylline Books' prophecy about 'the enemy of the Romans' as a promise.
I seized Rome in 306, and my memory was later officially condemned.
I drowned in the Tiber when my bridge of boats collapsed.

people.name: Maximian
clues: In 307 I married my daughter to the young emperor proclaimed at York.
My son seized Rome three months after his rival was proclaimed.
In 310 I rebelled against my own son-in-law.
Cornered at Marseille, I hanged myself.

places.name: Nicomedia
places.why: On a hill outside this city Diocletian was proclaimed emperor in 284 and stepped down in 305, and the Great Persecution began here.

places.name: Split
places.why: Diocletian retired to a fortified palace on the Dalmatian coast that is now the old heart of Split.

places.name: Alexandria
places.why: Egypt's great port, besieged by Diocletian after the revolt of 297 until it fell in 298.

places.name: Ctesiphon
places.why: The Persian capital on the Tigris, taken by Galerius in 298.

places.name: York
places.why: Constantine's father died here in 306 and the troops proclaimed Constantine Augustus.

places.name: Carnuntum
places.why: At this army town on the Danube Diocletian was begged to return to power in 308 and refused.

places.name: Naissus
places.why: Constantine was born here around AD 272.
